extracted.intended_audience: authors, editors, copyeditors, typesetters, and publishers
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial and typographic rules from The University of Chicago Manual of Style covering capitalization, use of italics, quotation marks, spelling/number rules, abbreviations, and related formatting for published material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-title capitalization (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: In foreign titles, in addition to capitalizing the first word, follow language-specific capitalization rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See subrules for Latin, French/Italian/Spanish/Swedish/Norwegian, German/Danish, and Dutch (items a–d). Examples: De amicitia; Histoire de la litterature frangaise; Geschichie des deutschen Feudalwesens; Geschiedenis der Nederlandsche Taal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-title capitalization: Latin
rubrics_metrics.description: In Latin titles, capitalize proper nouns and adjectives derived therefrom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: De amicitia, Bellum Gallicum.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-title capitalization: French/Italian/Spanish/Swedish/Norwegian
rubrics_metrics.description: In these languages, capitalize proper nouns but not adjectives derived from them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Histoire de la litterature frangaise; Novelle e racconti popolari italiani; Antologia de poelas liricos castellanos; Svenska litteraturens historic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-title capitalization: German/Danish
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize all nouns but not adjectives, except German adjectives derived from persons' names (which are capitalized).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Geschichte des deutschen Feudalwesens (but: die Homerische Frage); Videnskabens Fremskridt i del niUende Aarhimdrede.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign-title capitalization: Dutch
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize all nouns and adjectives derived from proper nouns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Geschiedenis der Nederlandsche Taal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definite article in publication titles
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not, as a rule, treat the definite article as part of the title when mentioning newspapers, magazines, and similar publications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use forms like the Chicago Tribune, the School Review, the Annual Register of the University of Chicago.

rubrics_metrics.name: Titles of ancient manuscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Titles of ancient manuscripts (singular MS; plural MSS) are capitalized as titles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Codex Bemensis, Cod. Canonicianus. (See also item 60 for related rules.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization in hyphenated title compounds
rubrics_metrics.description: In titles with main words capitalized, capitalize all nouns forming parts of hyphenated compounds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: "Twentieth-Century Progress," "The Economy of High-Speed Trains." Do not capitalize non-noun components. In side-heads, capitalize only the first word and proper nouns (see items 56 and 172).

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of scientific (Latin) taxonomic names
rubrics_metrics.description: In botanical, geological, zoological, and paleontological contexts, capitalize scientific (Latin) names of divisions, orders, families, and genera, but not their English derivatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Cotylosauria, but cotylosaurs; Felidae, but felids; Carnivora, but carnivores. Also guidance on species names: capitalize species derived from persons or from generic names in botanical/zoological contexts but not in geological/medical contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names and epithets of peoples, races, and tribes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Kafir, Negro (in its ethnic sense), Hottentot, Makassar, Buginese, Celestials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Astronomical names capitalization
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names of planets, stars, and groups of stars (but not 'sun', 'earth', 'moon', 'stars'); also capitalize designations of celestial objects in well-known catalogues and Flamsteed numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Saturn, Ursa Major, the Milky Way, M 13, N.G.C. 6165, 85 Pegasi, Lalande 5761.

rubrics_metrics.name: University divisions/offices/courses capitalization (institutional)
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize names, divisions, departments, officers, and courses of study of the University (in official administrative or curricular work).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the School of Education (the School), the Department of Anthropology (the Department), the Board of Trustees (the Trustees, the Board), Dean of the Faculties (the Faculty). Use the appropriate short forms when indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of capitals and small capitals in letters (date, salutatory, signature, residence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the names of town and state in the date line, salutatory phrase at beginning, and signature and residence at the end of letters in capitals and small capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chicago, Ill., January 1, 1911. My dear Mr. Smith: (set flush with a colon). Signature and residence set to the right with indention; address lines etc. have specific typographic positioning guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'Whereas', 'Note', and 'Section' in formal documents
rubrics_metrics.description: In resolutions use 'Whereas'; in notes (not footnotes) use 'Note.' followed by a period and dash; in constitutions/by-laws use 'Section' introducing paragraphs followed by a number.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Usual practice is to abbreviate 'Section' after the first occurrence (Section 1. ...; Sec 2. ...). Example: Note. — It should be noticed that ....

rubrics_metrics.name: Set A.M./P.M. and B.C./A.D. in small capitals
rubrics_metrics.description: Set A.M. and P.M. (ante and post meridiem) and B.C. and A.D. in small capitals and without spaces between letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 11:30 A.M.; 53 B.C., 1906 A.D. See other related rules for punctuation and abbreviation spacing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use lowercase initial letter for generalized former proper names
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a small (lower-case) initial letter for words of common usage originally proper names and their derivatives, and verbs derived from proper names (when origin is obscured).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: utopia, bohemian, philistine, titanic, platonic, quixotic, bonanza, china, morocco, guinea-pig, boycott, roman (type), italicize, anglicize, macadamize, paris green.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalize minor literary-reference subdivisions selectively
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, capitalize minor subdivisions and use standard abbreviations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: chapter, section, page, article, verse, line, note; chap., sec, p., art., vs., l., n. (See other items for cross-references.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviations for common units of measurement
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard abbreviations for units of measurement in references and lists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: h. = hour, min. = minute, sec. = second; lb. = pound, oz. = ounce; yd. = yard, ft. = foot; etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization in side-heads
rubrics_metrics.description: In side-heads (subheadings), capitalize only the first word and proper names.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related rules 56, 172, and 280 for exceptions and extended guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capitalization of first word of quotation connected to preceding text
rubrics_metrics.description: Capitalize the first word of a quotation that is immediately connected with what precedes, even if that word begins a sentence in the original.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See items 35 and 131 for further illustrations and exceptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize for emphasis
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words or phrases to which emphasis or importance is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'This was, however, not the case'; 'It is sufficiently plain that the sciences of life, at least, are studies of processes.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize foreign words/phrases not incorporated into English
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize foreign-language words and phrases inserted into English text and not adopted into English; and, as a rule, single sentences or brief passages not long enough for reduced type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'the Darwinian Weltanschauung'; 'Napoleon's coup d'etat'; 'de gustibus non est disputandum.' But do not italicize foreign titles preceding names or names of foreign institutions/places commonly used in English (e.g., Pere Lagrange, Reichstag).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not italicize anglicized everyday foreign words
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not italicize foreign words of everyday occurrence that have become sufficiently anglicized even if they retain accents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ad interim, confrere, erratum, addendum, connoisseur, et cetera, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize titles of publications (books, periodicals)
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize titles of publications including books (plays, essays, cycles of poems printed separately), pamphlets, treatises, tracts, documents, periodicals, proceedings/transactions, and journal names appearing in their own pages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Spencer, Principles of Sociology; A Midsummer-Night's Dream; Paradise Lost; the Modern Language Review; the Chicago Tribune. Note: exceptions for long bibliographical lists, tables, or contexts where italics would be excessive (see note to 41). Books of the Bible and titles of ancient manuscripts should be set in roman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize certain Latin/legal/literary abbreviations and words in references
rubrics_metrics.description: Italicize words/phrases/abbreviations used in literary and legal references such as ad loc, circa (ca.), et al., ibid., idem, infra, lac. cit., op. cit., passim, sic, sc, supra, s.v., vide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But do not italicize cf., e.g., i.e., V. or vs. (versus) unless ambiguity would result; viz., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize 'See'/'See also' for cross-references in indexes
rubrics_metrics.description: Use roman or italics to differentiate cross-reference words in indexes where desirable; italicize See/See also when differentiation is desired.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: See also Sociology; for levee read levee (used to separate correct/incorrect readings in errata lists).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize plaintiff/defendant names in legal citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Set the names of plaintiff and defendant in citations of legal causes in italics; likewise titles of proceedings containing prefixes like in re, ex parte, in the matter of, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Conolly v. Union Sewer Pipe Co.; In re Smith; Ex parte Brown.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address lines and primary address lines formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: Set address lines in speeches, reports, and primary address lines in letters flush in a separate line with nouns capitalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mr. President, Ladies and Gentlemen: / Mr. John Smith, 121 Dearborn Street, Chicago, Ill. / Dear Sir: I take pleasure in announcing ....

rubrics_metrics.name: Signatures: position/title formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: In signatures, set the position or title after the name; if one word, run into same line; if more than one word and no longer than the name, center first letter under name and indent one em on the right; if longer, center name over second line and set title flush.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Arthur P. Maguire, Secretary; Yours very truly, Carter H. Harrison; Charles M. Gayley / Professor of English Language and Literature. Rules are subject to special-case exigencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a), b), c) subdivisions and affixed letters
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a), b), c), etc., for paragraph subdivisions (single parenthesis if beginning a paragraph, double parentheses if run in); use letters a, b, c affixed to verse/page numbers to denote fractional parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Luke 4:31a.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters to designate unknown quantities
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters to designate unknown quantities, lines, etc., in algebraic, geometrical, and similar matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ac + bc = c(a + b); lines a/ and /I Z); the nth power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Letters in legends corresponding to illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Use letters in legends or text to refer to corresponding letters in accompanying illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'At the point A above (see diagram).'

rubrics_metrics.name: References to particular letters
rubrics_metrics.description: When referring to particular letters, use phrasing to indicate case/quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the letter u, a small v, a capital S.

rubrics_metrics.name: Shillings and pence notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use s. Sd. (shillings and pence) following numerals where appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 35s. 6d. (See item 270 for additional guidance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicize genus and species names in biological contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: In zoological, geological, and paleontological matter, italicize scientific (Latin) names of genera and species when used together, with the generic name in the nominative singular; in botanical contexts similar rules apply. In medical matter generally print such names in roman.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Felis leo, Rosa Carolina, Conodectes favosus, Phyteuma Halleri. See also related rules (46, 48).

rubrics_metrics.name: Italicization exceptions for scientific symbols and spectral notation
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not italicize symbols for chemical elements, Fraunhofer capital letters given to spectral lines, letters designating spectral types of stars, or hydrogen-line designations (use roman).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: H, Ca, Ti; A-H and K; As, B4, Mb; Ha, Hβ, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Resolved' in resolutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Start resolutions with the word 'Resolved.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See item 39 for related practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'Continued'/'To be continued' after headlines/titles
rubrics_metrics.description: After headlines or titles, as a rule, use the word 'Continued'; at ends of articles use 'To be continued.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: [To be continued]

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks: run-in citations
rubrics_metrics.description: Put citations run into the text (a passage quoted in the author's own words) between quotation marks and in roman type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See item 85 for exceptions where long quotations are set in smaller type without quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for consecutive quotations
rubrics_metrics.description: When quoting different authors or different works by same author in succession without intervening original matter, put each quotation in quotation marks even if reduced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See item 75 for specifics and reduced citation guidance items 85–87.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Place a word or phrase accompanied by its definition in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Drop-folio' means a page-number at the foot of the page.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for unusual/technical/ironical words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for unusual, technical, ironical, or highlighted words or phrases in the text, whether or not accompanied by words like 'so-called.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Her 'five o'clocks' were famous; He was elected 'master of the rolls'; the so-called 'man of affairs.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for translations
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclose the English equivalent of a foreign word/phrase with quotation marks when given as a translation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Weltanschauung, 'world-view' or 'fundamental aspect of life'; Romische Geschichte ('History of Rome').

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks to highlight particular words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks to indicate the particular word(s) being discussed or emphasized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the term 'lynch law'; the phrase 'liberty of conscience'; the concepts 'good' and 'bad'; the name 'Chicago.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for titles of book series
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclose titles of book series in quotation marks when cited in text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'English Men of Letters Series'; 'International Critical Commentary'; the series 'Handbooks of Ethics and Religion.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for shorter poems
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of shorter poems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Shelley's 'To a Skylark.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for cited titles of subdivisions and short works
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of subdivisions (parts, books, chapters), papers, lectures, sermons, articles, toasts, mottoes, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. I, 'The British School,' chap. ii, 'John Stuart Mill'; the articles 'Cross', 'Crucifixion.' Note: references to Preface, Introduction, Table of Contents, Index of a specific work should be set with capitals and without quotation marks (Preface, p. iii).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for names of ships
rubrics_metrics.description: Enclose the names of ships in quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the U.S. SS. 'Oregon.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotation marks for titles of pictures and works of art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Murillo's 'The Holy Family.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduced (set smaller) quotations rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Set prose extracts of five or more lines and poetry of two or more lines in smaller type; reduced citations ordinarily should not have quotation marks.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An isolated short prose quotation may be run into text if organically related. Use type-size reductions from ii-pt/10-pt to 9-pt, 9-pt to 8-pt, 8-pt to 6-pt (see 86). Reduced citations should not have quotation marks except in special cases (see 75).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quotation marks must include ellipses and 'etc.' when clarity requires
rubrics_metrics.description: Quotation marks should include ellipses and the phrase 'etc.' when they otherwise would not be clearly part of the quoted material; perfect clarity in each case is the best criterion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples illustrate when etc. belongs inside or outside quotes depending on whether it indicates omitted material or is commentary outside the quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeat quotation marks at beginnings of quoted paragraphs
rubrics_metrics.description: If quoted prose broken into paragraphs is enclosed in quotation marks, repeat the quotation marks at the beginning of each paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensures clarity for multi-paragraph quotations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear alignment of quotation marks when alignment is desired
rubrics_metrics.description: When alignment is desired, clear the quotation marks so they project beyond the line of alignment (i.e., let the marks extend slightly to visually align text).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example demonstrates visual alignment with projecting quotation marks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of double and single quotation marks nesting
rubrics_metrics.description: Use double quotation marks for primary quotations and single marks for a quotation within a quotation, alternating for additional nested quotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pattern: double → single → double → single, etc. Examples provided with multi-level quoting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out titles of honor and forms of address preceding names
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out all religious, civil, and military titles of honor and respect and forms of address preceding the name, except Mr., Messrs., Mrs., Dr., Rev., Hon. (with exceptions noted for Rev. and Hon. in certain contexts); abbreviate Esq. following the name.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: French equivalents exceptions noted (M., MM., Mme, Mlle). In quotations and correspondence different practices may apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out Christian (given) names
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out Christian (given) names (e.g., George, Charles, John) rather than abbreviating (Geo., Chas.), except when the abbreviated form occurs in quoted matter or original signatures; also spell out von as part of a name (see 240).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid abbreviations of given names in ordinary text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out numbers of less than three digits in ordinary prose
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary reading matter, spell out numbers of less than three digits, unless statistical/technical or part of a close succession of six or more numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'There are thirty-eight cities...' 'a fifty-yard dash'; exceptions include dimensions, degrees, decimals, enumerations, money, percentage, weights which should generally be expressed in figures (10°, 45 miles, $1,000).

rubrics_metrics.name: Express round numbers in words
rubrics_metrics.description: Use words for round, approximate figures (unit being 100 for numbers under 1,000 and 1,000 for larger numbers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'The attendance was estimated at five hundred' (but 'at 550'); 'a thesis of about three thousand words' (but 'of about 2,700'). If spelling out 1,500, use 'fifteen hundred.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Spell out numbers that begin sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: All numbers, no matter how large, that begin a sentence in ordinary prose should be spelled out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Five hundred and ninety-three men, 417 women, and 126 children...' If impracticable, reconstruct the sentence to avoid beginning with numerals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sums of money in ordinary prose spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: When sums of money occur in isolated cases in ordinary reading matter, spell them out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'The admission was two dollars.' For several numbers occurring close together or in statistical matter, use figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time of day in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: In ordinary prose write times in words (at four; at half-past two in the afternoon; at seven o'clock). In statistical/enumerative contexts and with A.M./P.M. use figures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statistically use at 4:15 P.M. (omit 'o'clock' in such contexts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ages in prose
rubrics_metrics.description: Express ages in words in ordinary text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: eighty years and four months old; children between six and fourteen.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numbers for centuries and similar designations spelled out
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out numbers of centuries, Egyptian dynasties, sessions of Congress, military bodies, political divisions, thoroughfares, and similar cases unless brevity is important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: nineteenth century; Fifth Dynasty; Fifty-fourth Congress, second session; Fifth Avenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: References to decades phrasing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use phrases like 'in the nineties' for references to particular decades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See related guidance (item 165) for additional conventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Names of months spelled out (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out names of months except in statistical matter or long enumerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: from January 1 to April 15 (omit st, d, th after dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of 'United States'
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out 'United States' except in quotations and certain connections (e.g., military/regimental abbreviations, ship names, footnotes, and similar references).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: General Schofield, U.S.A.; U.S. SS. 'Oregon'; in footnotes: U.S. Geological Survey.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spelling out 'Railroad (-way)', 'Fort', 'Mount', 'Port' in geographic names
rubrics_metrics.description: Spell out words like 'Railroad' (or -way), 'Fort', 'Mount', 'Port' in geographical appellations rather than abbreviating.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad (not R.R. or Ry.); Fort Wayne, Mount Elias, Port Huron.

rubrics_metrics.name: General rule for names of publications
rubrics_metrics.description: In most cases spell out the names of publications; modify based on expediency, context, authoritative usage, and author's preference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If in doubt, spell out. Good taste tolerates offenses in spelling out more readily than the opposite.

rubrics_metrics.name: State abbreviations in bibliographical/technical contexts
rubrics_metrics.description: Abbreviate names of states, territories, and possessions following towns in lists, bibliographical matter, etc., using standardized abbreviations without spaces between letters; do not ordinarily abbreviate in running text.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List includes Ala., Alaska, Ariz., Ark., Cal., Colo., Conn., Del., Fla., Ga., Ida., Ill., Ind., Iowa, Kan., Ky., La., Me., Md., Mass., Mich., Minn., Miss., Mo., Mont., Neb., Nev., N.H., N.J., N.M., N.Y., N.C., N.D., Ohio, Okla., Ore., Pa., R.I., S.C., S.D., Tenn., Tex., Utah, Vt., Va., Wash., W.Va., Wis., Wyo., plus territorial abbreviations like P.I., P.R., T.H., D.C.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use ampersand in technical/bibliographic names
rubrics_metrics.description: In technical matter (footnotes, bibliographies), abbreviate 'Company' and 'Brothers' and use '&' in commercial firm names; in running text spell these out when the firm name consists of common words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Macmillan Co., Macmillan & Co., Harper Bros.; Chicago, Milwaukee & St. Paul Railroad. In text: American Steel and Wire Co.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abbreviate 'Saint' as 'St.' in place names (with exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'St.' for 'Saint' before a name in many place names, but preferably omit 'St.' when referring to apostles, evangelists, and church fathers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: St. Louis, St. Peter's Church; but Luke, Paul, Augustine (not St. Luke, St. Paul).

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard abbreviations for books of the Bible and apocrypha
rubrics_metrics.description: Use standard short forms for the books of the Bible, Apocrypha, and commonly referred-to versions of the Bible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensive lists provided for Old Testament and New Testament books (Gen., Exod., Lev., Num., Deut., Josh., etc.), Apocrypha (I and II Esd., Wisd. of Sol., Tob.), and versions (A.V. = Authorized Version, R.V. = Revised Version, A.R.V. = American Standard Revised Version, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliographical abbreviations: vol., no., p., pp., fig., ed.
rubrics_metrics.description: In literary references, footnotes, and bibliographical contexts use standard abbreviations for volume, number, psalm, division, chapter, article, section, page, column, verse, line, note, figure, edition, and continuation indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Vol. I (Vols.), No. 1 (Nos.), Ps. 20 (Pss.), Div. III, chap. ii (chaps.), art. iii (arts.), sec. 4 (secs.), p. 5 (pp.), col. 6 (cols.), vs. 7 (vss.), l. 8 (ll.), n. 9 (nn.), Fig. 7 (Figs.); pp. 5–7, pp. sf., pp. 5 ff., ed(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: Metric and other unit abbreviation conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use commonly accepted abbreviations for metric and other units when following numerals in technical contexts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 1 m., 2 dm., 3 cm., 4 mm.; cm. (cubic meter), c.c., cu.; sq. mi., gm. (gram), gr. (grain), h. (hour), min., sec., lb., oz., yd., ft., in.; kg., kw., mg., mag., A (angstrom), h.p., C. (Centigrade), F. (Fahrenheit). See note on hyphenated abbreviations: first element takes no period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standard technical abbreviations recommended by American Institute of Electrical Engineers
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the recommended list of technical abbreviations for electrical engineering values in technical documents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include a-c. (alternating current used as compound adjective), b.h.p. (brake horse-power), B.t.u., c-p. (candle-power), cm., cir. mils, counter e.m.f., cu., d-c., e.h.p., e.m.f., ft., ft-lb., gal., gr-, g. or gm., g-cal., hr., in., i.h.p., kg., kg-m., km., kw., kw-hr., m., m-kg., m.m.f., m.p.hr. (sec.), mm., mg., min., rev. per min., sec., sq., kv., kv-a., watt-hr., yd., etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use office style for modern-author extracts except where fidelity required
rubrics_metrics.description: In extracts from modern authors whose spelling and punctuation differ only slightly from modern usage, convert to office style when variations do not affect meaning; follow original in Old English works or where essential to context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Titles should always be accurately quoted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forming possessive of names ending in sibilant
rubrics_metrics.description: Form the possessive of proper names ending in s or another sibilant: if monosyllabic, add apostrophe and s; if multisyllabic, add apostrophe only, except for names ending in -ce.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: King James's Version, Burns's poems, Marx's theories; Moses' law, Jesus' birth, Demosthenes' orations. For silent sibilants, always add apostrophe and s: Charlevoix's discoveries, Des Moines's population.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of indefinite article 'a' before sounded h and long u/eu and words 'one/once'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'a' (not 'an') before words beginning with a sounded h, long u (or eu), and before the words 'one' and 'once'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a hotel, a harmonic rendition, a historical work, a union, a euphonious word, such a one.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using Latin/Greek ligatures
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not use ligatures (æ and œ) in modern English usage; write ae/oe separately or with e alone, except retain ligatures in Old English and French usages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: aetas; Oedipus Tyrannus; aesthetic; but oeuvre (French); maneuver; Alfred (English form).

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate 'farther' and 'further'
rubrics_metrics.description: Use 'farther' for physical distance ('more remote') and 'further' for figurative or additional sense ('moreover', 'in addition').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the farther end; he went still farther; further, he suggested; a further reason.
